writing.explanation:
In triangle 0-1-2-0, DFS ignores each immediate parent edge but finds an already seen non-parent vertex on the remaining edge. A star has no such edge. This implementation's contract excludes parallel edges and self-loops.

The worked program is a complete executable for this pattern. Its core function uses typed input so the state transitions remain visible. The challenge input contract is: Return true when the undirected graph contains a cycle. The visible fixture is `edges=(0,1),(1,2),(2,0),(2,3)` and its example result is `true`. The implementation and additional semantic fixtures were checked against an independent reference calculation. Those bounded tests establish these examples; they are not a proof for all inputs or a measurement on an iPhone.

Return a canonical String from solve: lowercase true/false for booleans; decimal integers without extra signs, leading zeros or whitespace; comma-separated sequence values and semicolon-separated groups. Whole-number medians have no decimal suffix; half medians use .5. Do not append a newline to the returned value. Preserve the explicitly named textual sentinels such as none or #. Input fixtures are bounded so the demonstrated arithmetic fits its named Rust types; satisfy the stated input preconditions before applying the algorithm.

String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

A problem is a good match for Undirected Cycle Detection when it asks for valid-tree checks and redundant connections. Here the concrete task is: Return true when the undirected graph contains a cycle. The visible input `edges=(0,1),(1,2),(2,0),(2,3)` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Choose a representation for the operations first; when traversing, DFS explores depth and BFS follows equal-cost layers. Directed edges and disconnected components change the plan. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: During traversal ignore the edge back to the parent; any other seen neighbor closes a cycle. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? A graph method needs an explicit vertex-and-edge representation. For traversal, define when a vertex becomes seen: on insertion into the frontier or on removal. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(V+E) time · O(V) space; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `true` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Test an isolated vertex, a cycle, duplicate edges, and a graph whose starting vertex reaches only one component. An adjacency list and `VecDeque` make breadth-first work explicit. Mark before enqueuing to avoid duplicate frontier entries. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
